Abstract.

New and old results on closed polynomials, i.e., such polynomials f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk that the subalgebra 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], are collected in the paper. Using some properties of closed polynomials we prove the following factorization theorem: Let f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk, where 𝕜\Bbbk is algebraically closed. Then for all but finite number μ∈𝕜\mu\in\Bbbk the polynomial f+μf+\mu can be decomposed into a product f+μ=α⋅f1​μ⋅f2​μ⋯fk​μ,α∈𝕜×,k⩾1f+\mu=\alpha\cdot f_{1\mu}\cdot f_{2\mu}\cdots f_{k\mu},\ \alpha\in\Bbbk^{\times},k\geqslant 1, of irreducible polynomials fi​μf_{i\mu} of the same degree dd not depending on μ\mu and such that fi​μ−fj​μ∈𝕜,i,j=1,…,k.f_{i\mu}-f_{j\mu}\in\Bbbk,\quad i,j=1,\ldots,k. An algorithm for finding of a generative polynomial of a given polynomial ff, which is a closed polynomial hh with f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) for some F⁡(t)∈𝕜⁡[t]F(t)\in\Bbbk[t], is given. Some types of saturated subalgebras A⊂𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]A\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] are considered, i.e., such that for any f∈A∖𝕜f\in A\setminus\Bbbk a generative polynomial of ff is contained in AA.

Key words and phrases: 
Polynomials, Integrally Closed Subalgebras, Derivations

1. Introduction

Recall that a polynomial f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk is called closed if the subalgebra 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. It turns out that a polynomial ff is closed if and only if ff is non-composite, i.e., cannot be presented in the form f=F⁡(g)f=F(g) for some g∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] and F⁡(t)∈𝕜⁡[t],deg⁡(F)>1.F(t)\in\Bbbk[t],\ \deg(F)>1. Because any polynomial in nn variables can be obtained from a closed polynomial by taking a polynomial in one variable from it, the problem of studying closed polynomials is of interest. Besides, closed polynomials in two variables appear in a natural way as generators of rings of constants of non-zero derivations.

In this paper we present some characterizations and properties of closed polynomials. They allow us to obtain a ”generic decomposition” of a polynomial f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] over an algebraically closed field 𝕜\Bbbk (Theorem 3), which may be considered as an analogue of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra for polynomials in many variables.

Let us go briefly through the content of the paper. In Section 2 we collect numerous characterizations of closed polynomials (Theorem 1). A major part of these characterizations is contained in the union of [1], [12], [14], [15], [16], etc, but some results seem to be new. In particular, implication (i) ⇒\Rightarrow (iv) in Theorem 1 over any perfect field and Proposition 2 solve a problem stated in [1, Sec. 8]. For all implications in Theorem 1 we give complete and elementary proofs.

Define a generative polynomial hh of a polynomial f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk as a closed polynomial such that f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) for some F∈𝕜⁡[t]F\in\Bbbk[t]. Clearly, a generative polynomial exists for any ff. Theorem 1 implies that a generative polynomial is unique up to affine transformations.

The above-mentioned results allow us to prove that over an algebraically closed field 𝕜\Bbbk for any f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk and for all but finite number μ∈𝕜\mu\in\Bbbk the polynomial f+μf+\mu can be decomposed into a product f+μ=α⋅f1​μ⋅f2​μ⋯fk​μ,α∈𝕜×,k⩾1f+\mu=\alpha\cdot f_{1\mu}\cdot f_{2\mu}\cdots f_{k\mu},\ \alpha\in\Bbbk^{\times},k\geqslant 1, of irreducible polynomials fi​μf_{i\mu} of the same degree dd not depending on μ\mu and such that fi​μ−fj​μ∈𝕜,i,j=1,…,kf_{i\mu}-f_{j\mu}\in\Bbbk,\ i,j=1,\ldots,k. Moreover, Stein-Lorenzini-Najib’s Inequality (Theorem 2) implies that the number of ”exceptional” values of μ\mu is less then deg⁡(f)\deg(f). The same inequality gives an estimate of the number of irreducible factors in f+μf+\mu for exceptional μ\mu, see Theorem 3.

Section 4 is devoted to saturated subalgebras A⊂𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]A\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], i.e., such that for any f∈A∖𝕜f\in A\setminus\Bbbk a generative polynomial of ff is contained in AA. Clearly, any subalgebra that is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is saturated. On the other hand, it is known that for monomial subalgebras these two conditions are equivalent. In Theorem 4 we characterize subalgebras of invariants A=𝕜​[x1,…,xn]GA=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}, where GG is a finite group acting linearly on 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], with AA being saturated. This result provides many examples of saturated homogeneous subalgebras that are not integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

In the last section we give an algorithm for finding a generative polynomial of a given polynomial ff. In particular, this provides a test to determine whether a given polynomial is closed.

2. Characterizations of closed polynomials

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be a field.

Definition 1.

A polynomial f⁡(x1,…,xn)∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk is called closed if the subalgebra 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Definition 2.

A polynomial f⁡(x1,…,xn)∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk is said to be non-composite if the condition

(*) there exist F⁡(t)∈𝕜⁡[t]F(t)\in\Bbbk[t] and g⁡(x1,…,xn)∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]g(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that

f⁡(x1,…,xn)=F⁡(g⁡(x1,…,xn))f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=F(g(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}))

implies deg⁡(F)=1\deg(F)=1.

Without loss of generality, we assume below that the leading coefficient of ff (say, with respect to the lexicographic order, x1>⋯>xnx_{1}>\dots>x_{n}) equals 1.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the set of all subalgebras 𝕜⁡[f],f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜\Bbbk[f],\ f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk, partially ordered by inclusion.

Theorem 1.

The following conditions on a polynomial f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    ff is non-composite;

  2. (ii)

    𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] is a maximal element of ℳ\mathcal{M};

  3. (iii)

    ff is closed;

  4. (iv)

    (𝕜\Bbbk is a perfect field) f+λf+\lambda is irreducible over 𝕜¯\overline{\Bbbk} for all but finitely many λ∈𝕜¯\lambda\in\overline{\Bbbk};

  5. (v)

    (𝕜\Bbbk is a perfect field) there exists λ∈𝕜¯\lambda\in\overline{\Bbbk} such that f+λf+\lambda is irreducible over 𝕜¯\overline{\Bbbk};

  6. (vi)

    (char​𝕜=0{\rm char\ }\Bbbk=0) there exists a (finite) family of derivations {Di}\{D_{i}\} of the algebra 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that 𝕜⁡[f]=∩Keri⁡Di\Bbbk[f]=\cap_{i}\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}D_{i}.

Proof.

Implications (iii) ⇒\Rightarrow (ii) ⇒\Rightarrow (i) are obvious.

(i) ⇒\Rightarrow (iii). It is sufficient to prove the following

Proposition 1.

For any f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk, the integral closure AA of 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] has the form A=𝕜⁡[h]A=\Bbbk[h] for some h∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Proof.

Here we follow [5] and [21]. Since any non-zero prime ideal of 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] is maximal, this also holds for AA.

Lemma 1.

The 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra AA may be realized as a 𝕜\Bbbk-subalgebra of a polynomial algebra in one variable.

Proof.

By definition, A⊂𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]A\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. If n=1n=1, then we are done. If n>1n>1, take r≫0r\gg 0 such that there exists a∈Aa\in A with a+λ∉I:=(xn+x1r)⊲𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]a+\lambda\notin I:=(x_{n}+x_{1}^{r})\lhd\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] for any λ∈𝕜\lambda\in\Bbbk. Here II is a prime ideal of 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], I∩AI\cap A is a prime ideal of AA, and since the image of AA in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]/I≅𝕜⁡[x1^,…,xn−1^]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]/I\cong\Bbbk[\widehat{x_{1}},\dots,\widehat{x_{n-1}}] is not a field, the ideal I∩AI\cap A is zero. This shows that AA is embedded into 𝕜⁡[x1^,…,xn−1^]\Bbbk[\widehat{x_{1}},\dots,\widehat{x_{n-1}}], and we may proceed by induction on nn. ∎

Note that since 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is integrally closed, the subalgebra AA is integrally closed too.

Lemma 2.

Let AA be an integrally closed subalgebra of 𝕜⁡[y]\Bbbk[y]. Then A=𝕜⁡[u]A=\Bbbk[u] for some u∈𝕜⁡[y]u\in\Bbbk[y].

Proof.

Let us assume that A≠𝕜A\neq\Bbbk. Let KK be the quotient field of AA. The algebra 𝕜⁡[y]\Bbbk[y] is integral over AA and K∩𝕜⁡[y]=AK\cap\Bbbk[y]=A. Consider an element u=u⁡(y)∈Au=u(y)\in A of the smallest possible positive degree m=deg⁡u⁡(y)m=\deg u(y). Take a variable tt over KK and consider a polynomial F⁡(y,t)=u⁡(t)−u⁡(y)∈K⁡[t]F(y,t)=u(t)-u(y)\in K[t]. If F⁡(y,t)=p⁡(y,t)​q​(y,t)F(y,t)=p(y,t)q(y,t), then we may assume that the highest coefficients of p⁡(y,t)p(y,t) and q⁡(y,t)q(y,t) are in 𝕜\Bbbk. Moreover, p⁡(y,t)p(y,t) and q⁡(y,t)q(y,t) are in 𝕜⁡[y,t]\Bbbk[y,t], because one may consider F=p​qF=pq as a decomposition in 𝕜​(y)​[t]\Bbbk(y)[t]. This shows that the coefficients of pp and qq are in AA.

Fix the lexicographic monomial order with y>ty>t. Then the leading term of F⁡(y,t)F(y,t) does not depend on tt. So this is the case for pp and qq. By minimality of deg⁡u⁡(y)\deg u(y), either pp or qq is a constant. This proves that F⁡(y,t)F(y,t) is irreducible in K⁡[t]K[t], and [𝕜(y):𝕜(u)]=m[\Bbbk(y):\Bbbk(u)]=m. On the other hand, if [𝕜(y):K]=d[\Bbbk(y):K]=d, then a linear combination of yd,…,y,1y^{d},\dots,y,1 is contained in K∩𝕜⁡[y]=AK\cap\Bbbk[y]=A, so d≥md\geq m. Hence K=𝕜⁡(u)K=\Bbbk(u) and 𝕜⁡[u]⊆A⊂𝕜⁡(u)\Bbbk[u]\subseteq A\subset\Bbbk(u). If F1​(u)F2​(u)∈A\frac{F_{1}(u)}{F_{2}(u)}\in A with coprime polynomials F1,F2F_{1},F_{2}, then there exist polynomials F3,F4F_{3},F_{4} such that F1​F3+F2​F4=1F_{1}F_{3}+F_{2}F_{4}=1, and F3​F1F2+F4=1F2∈AF_{3}\frac{F_{1}}{F_{2}}+F_{4}=\frac{1}{F_{2}}\in A. But AA contains no non-constant invertible elements. This proves that A=𝕜⁡[u]A=\Bbbk[u]. ∎

(iv) ⇒\Rightarrow (v) is obvious, since 𝕜¯\overline{\Bbbk} is infinite.

(v) ⇒\Rightarrow (i). If f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) and F⁡(t)+λ=(t−α1)​…​(t−αk)F(t)+\lambda=(t-\alpha_{1})\dots(t-\alpha_{k}) with α1,…,αk∈𝕜¯\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k}\in\overline{\Bbbk}, then f+λ=(h−α1)​…​(h−αk)f+\lambda=(h-\alpha_{1})\dots(h-\alpha_{k}).

(i) ⇒\Rightarrow (iv). Let us assume that 𝕜=𝕜¯\Bbbk=\overline{\Bbbk}. Consider a morphism ϕ:𝕜n→𝕜1\phi:\Bbbk^{n}\to\Bbbk^{1}, ϕ⁡(x1,…,xn)=f⁡(x1,…,xn)\phi(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})=f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). We are going to prove that all fibers of this morphism except for finitely many are irreducible. It follows from the next theorem (see, for example, [17, p. 139]).

The first Bertini theorem. Let XX and YY be irreducible algebraic varieties and ϕ:X→Y\phi:X\to Y be a dominant morphism. Suppose that the subfield ϕ∗​(𝕜​(Y))\phi^{*}(\Bbbk(Y)) is algebraically closed in 𝕜⁡(X)\Bbbk(X). Then there exists a non-empty open subset U⊂YU\subset Y such that all fibers ϕ−1​(y)\phi^{-1}(y) over y∈Uy\in U are irreducible.

So we need only to prove the following lemma.

Lemma 3.

Let f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk. The subfield 𝕜⁡(f)\Bbbk(f) is algebraically closed in 𝕜⁡(x1,…,xn)\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) if and only if ff is a closed polynomial.

Proof.

If f=F⁡(h)f=F(h), then hh is in the algebraic closure of 𝕜⁡(f)\Bbbk(f). Conversely, suppose that for an element g∈𝕜⁡(x1,…,xn)g\in\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) one has an equation

b0​gm+b1​gm−1+⋯+bm=0b_{0}g^{m}+b_{1}g^{m-1}+\dots+b_{m}=0

with bi∈𝕜⁡[f]b_{i}\in\Bbbk[f]. Then b0​gb_{0}g is integral over 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f], and, since ff is closed, one has b0​g∈𝕜⁡[f]b_{0}g\in\Bbbk[f]. This shows that g∈𝕜⁡(f)g\in\Bbbk(f). ∎

Finally, if 𝕜\Bbbk is a non-closed perfect field, the next proposition shows that f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is closed over 𝕜\Bbbk implies that ff is closed over 𝕜¯\overline{\Bbbk}.

Proposition 2.

Let f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk and 𝕜⊂L\Bbbk\subset L be a separable extension of fields. Then ff is closed over 𝕜\Bbbk if and only if ff is closed over LL.

Proof.

If f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) over 𝕜\Bbbk, then the same decomposition holds over LL.

Now assume that ff is closed over 𝕜\Bbbk. Consider an element g∈L⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in L[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] integral over L⁡[f]L[f]. We shall prove that g∈L⁡[f]g\in L[f]. Since the number of non-zero coefficients of gg is finite, we may assume that LL is a finitely generated extension of 𝕜\Bbbk. Then there exists a finite separable transcendence basis of LL over 𝕜\Bbbk, i.e., a finite set {ξ1,…,ξm}\{\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{m}\} of elements in LL that are algebraically independent over 𝕜\Bbbk and LL is a finite separable algebraic extension of L1=𝕜⁡(ξ1,…​ξm)L_{1}=\Bbbk(\xi_{1},\dots\xi_{m}).

Let us show that ff is closed over L1L_{1}. The subalgebra 𝕜⁡[f]​[ξ1,…,ξm]\Bbbk[f][\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{m}] is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]​[ξ1,…,ξm]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}][\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{m}] [3, Ch. V.1, Prop. 12]. Let TT be the set of all non-zero elements of 𝕜⁡[ξ1,…,ξm]\Bbbk[\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{m}]. Then the localization T−1​𝕜​[f]​[ξ1,…,ξm]T^{-1}\Bbbk[f][\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{m}] is integrally closed in T−1​𝕜​[x1,…,xn]​[ξ1,…​ξm]T^{-1}\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}][\xi_{1},\dots\xi_{m}] [3, Ch. V.1, Prop. 16]. This proves that L1​[f]L_{1}[f] is integrally closed in L1​[x1,…,xn]L_{1}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Fix a basis {ω1,…,ωk}\{\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{k}\} of LL over L1L_{1}. With any element l∈Ll\in L one may associate a L1L_{1}-linear operator M⁡(l):L→LM(l):L\to L, M​(l)​(ω)=l​ωM(l)(\omega)=l\omega. Let tr(l)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(l) be the trace of this operator. It is known that there exists a basis {ω1⋆,…,ωk⋆}\{\omega_{1}^{\star},\dots,\omega_{k}^{\star}\} of LL over L1L_{1} such that tr(ωi​ωj⋆)=δi​j\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\omega_{i}\omega_{j}^{\star})=\delta_{ij} [3, Ch. V.1.6]. Assume that g=∑iωi​aig=\sum_{i}\omega_{i}a_{i} with ai∈L1​[x1,…,xn]a_{i}\in L_{1}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. Any ωj⋆\omega_{j}^{\star} is integral over L1L_{1} and thus over L1​[f]L_{1}[f]. This shows that g​ωj⋆g\omega_{j}^{\star} is integral over L1​[f]L_{1}[f]. Set K=L1​(x1,…,xn)K=L_{1}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). The element g​ωj⋆g\omega_{j}^{\star} determines a KK-linear map L⊗KK→L⊗KKL\otimes_{K}K\to L\otimes_{K}K, b→g​ωj⋆​bb\to g\omega_{j}^{\star}b. Since g​ωj⋆g\omega_{j}^{\star} is integral over L1​[f]L_{1}[f], the trace of this KK-linear operator is also integral over L1​[f]L_{1}[f] [3, Ch. V.1.6]. Note that tr(g​ωj⋆)=∑iai​tr(ωi​ωj⋆)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(g\omega_{j}^{\star})=\sum_{i}a_{i}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\omega_{i}\omega_{j}^{\star}). On the other hand, the elements {ω1⊗1,…,ωk⊗1}\{\omega_{1}\otimes 1,\dots,\omega_{k}\otimes 1\} form a basis of L⊗KKL\otimes_{K}K over KK. Hence tr(ωi​ωj⋆)=δi​j\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(\omega_{i}\omega_{j}^{\star})=\delta_{ij} and tr(g​ωj⋆)=aj\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(g\omega_{j}^{\star})=a_{j} is integral over L1​[f]L_{1}[f]. This shows that aj∈L1​[f]a_{j}\in L_{1}[f] for any jj and thus g∈L⁡[f]g\in L[f]. ∎

Example 1.

If the field 𝕜\Bbbk is not perfect, then we can not guarantee that a polynomial ff which closed over 𝕜\Bbbk, will be closed over 𝕜¯\overline{\Bbbk} as well. Indeed, let F=𝕜⁡(η)F=\Bbbk(\eta) with η∉𝕜\eta\notin\Bbbk, ηp∈𝕜\eta^{p}\in\Bbbk. The polynomial f⁡(x1,x2)=x1p+ηp​x2pf(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}^{p}+\eta^{p}x_{2}^{p} is closed over 𝕜\Bbbk. However, one has a decomposition f=(x1+η​x2)pf=(x_{1}+\eta x_{2})^{p} over FF. The same example works for (i) ⇏\not\Rightarrow (iv) in this case.

(vi) ⇒\Rightarrow (iii). It is easy to check that for any derivation D:𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]→𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]D:\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\to\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the kernel KerD\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}D is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], and so is the intersection of kernels.

(i) ⇒\Rightarrow (vi). For any 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n consider a derivation

Di​j=∂f∂xi​∂∂xj−∂f∂xj​∂∂xi.D_{ij}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{j}}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{j}}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_{i}}.

Clearly, f∈Ker(Di​j)f\in\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}(D_{ij}). The following Lemmas show that for a closed ff one has 𝕜[f]=∩1≤i<j≤nDi​j\Bbbk[f]=\cap_{1\leq i<j\leq n}D_{ij}.

Lemma 4.

Assume that char𝕜=0\mathop{\mathrm{char}}\Bbbk=0. Polynomials f,g∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f,g\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk are algebraically dependent (over 𝕜\Bbbk) if and only if the rank of their Jacoby matrix

J⁡(f,g)=(∂f∂x1⋯∂f∂xn∂g∂x1⋯∂g∂xn)J(f,g)=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{n}}\\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_{1}}&\cdots&\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_{n}}\end{array}\right)

equals to 1,1, i.e.,

|∂f∂xi∂f∂xj∂g∂xi∂g∂xj|=0,i,j=1,…,n.\left|\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}}&\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{j}}\\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_{i}}&\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_{j}}\end{array}\right|=0,\quad i,j=1,\ldots,n.
Proof.

See [7, Ch. 3, Th. III] or [18, Cor. 2]. ∎

Lemma 5.

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be a field. Polynomials f,g∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f,g\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk are algebraically dependent (over 𝕜\Bbbk) if and only if there exists a closed polynomial h∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] such that f,g∈𝕜⁡[h]f,g\in\Bbbk[h].

Proof.

Assume that f,gf,g are algebraically dependent. By the Noether Normalization Lemma, there exists an element r∈𝕜⁡[f,g]r\in\Bbbk[f,g] such that 𝕜⁡[r]⊂𝕜⁡[f,g]\Bbbk[r]\subset\Bbbk[f,g] is an integral extension. By Proposition 1, the integral closure of 𝕜⁡[r]\Bbbk[r] in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] has a form 𝕜⁡[h]\Bbbk[h] for some closed polynomial hh.

Conversely, if f,g∈k⁡[h]f,g\in k[h] then these polynomials are obviously algebraically dependent. ∎

This completes the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

Remark 1.

Condition (vi) may be strengthened. It is proved in [13] (see also [2]) that in characteristic zero for any family of 𝕜\Bbbk-derivations {Di}\{D_{i}\} of a finitely generated 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra AA without zero divisors there exists a 𝕜\Bbbk-derivation DD of AA with KerD=∩Keri⁡Di\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}D=\cap_{i}\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}D_{i}.

Definition 3.

Let f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk. A closed polynomial h∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is called a generative polynomial of ff, if there exists F∈𝕜⁡[t]F\in\Bbbk[t] such that f=F⁡(h)f=F(h).

Corollary 1.

Let f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk. The integral closure of the subalgebra 𝕜⁡[f]\Bbbk[f] in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] coincides with 𝕜⁡[h]\Bbbk[h], where hh is a generative polynomial of ff. In particular, a generative polynomial of ff exists and is unique up to affine transformations.

Remark 2.

If one assumes that a generative polynomial hh of ff satisfies h⁡(0,…,0)=0h(0,\dots,0)=0 and the leading coefficient of hh equals 1, then such a generative polynomial exists and is unique. Below we shall consider generative polynomials under these assumptions.

We refer to [1] for numerous examples and interesting classes of closed polynomials.

Remark 3.
  1. (1)

    Let BB be an affine 𝕜\Bbbk-algebra and again ℳ⁡(B)\mathcal{M}(B) be the set of all subalgebras 𝕜⁡[b],b∈B∖𝕜\Bbbk[b],\ b\in B\setminus\Bbbk, partially ordered by inclusion. It follows from the proof above that if BB is integrally closed and there exists an embedding of BB into a polynomial algebra, then any element b∈B∖𝕜b\in B\setminus\Bbbk is contained in a unique maximal element of ℳ⁡(B)\mathcal{M}(B). For example, consider B=𝕜⁡[x,y]/(y2−x3−x−1)B=\Bbbk[x,y]/(y^{2}-x^{3}-x-1). Here y2∈𝕜⁡[x]∩𝕜⁡[y]y^{2}\in\Bbbk[x]\cap\Bbbk[y], thus BB can not be embedded into a polynomial algebra.

  2. (2)

    Let us recall that a subalgebra BB in AA is called algebraically closed if any element of AA that is algebraic over BB is contained in BB. It follows from Lemma 5 that a subalgebra 𝕜⁡[f]⊂𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[f]\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is algebraically closed if and only if it is integrally closed. For an arbitrary subalgebra this is no longer true (take 𝕜⁡[x,x​y]⊂𝕜⁡[x,y]\Bbbk[x,xy]\subset\Bbbk[x,y]).

  3. (3)

    If a subalgebra B⊂𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]B\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is 2-generated, then one can not bound the number of generators of its integral closure AA in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. For example, it is easy to check that for B=𝕜⁡[x1,x1​x2m]B=\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{1}x_{2}^{m}] the minimal number of generators of A=𝕜⁡[x1,x1​x2,…,x1​x2m]A=\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{1}x_{2},\dots,x_{1}x_{2}^{m}] is m+1m+1.

Finally, let us give one more observation following from Theorem 1. Denote by PP the set of all irreducible polynomials from 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] and consider the binary relation on this set: f≃g⟺∃c1∈𝕜×,c2∈𝕜:f=c1​g+c2.f\simeq g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\exists c_{1}\in\Bbbk^{\times},c_{2}\in\Bbbk:f=c_{1}g+c_{2}. It is easy to see that ≃\simeq is an equivalence relation. Choose arbitrarily a polynomial from each equivalence class and denote by π\pi the set of such polynomials.

Corollary 2.

There is a decomposition 𝕜[x1,…,xn]=∪p∈π𝕜[p],\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]=\cup_{p\in\pi}\Bbbk[p], where 𝕜⁡[pi]∩𝕜⁡[pj]=𝕜\Bbbk[p_{i}]\cap\Bbbk[p_{j}]=\Bbbk for all pi,pj∈πp_{i},p_{j}\in\pi, pi≠pjp_{i}\neq p_{j}.

The set of nonconstant polynomials in one variable 𝕜⁡[t]∖𝕜\Bbbk[t]\setminus\Bbbk forms a semigroup relatively to composition of polynomials (f∘g)​(t)=f⁡(g⁡(t))(f\circ g)(t)=f(g(t)). This semigroup acts naturally on the set of nonconstant polynomials 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk by the rule f⁡(h)=f⁡(h⁡(x1,…,xn))f(h)=f(h(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})) for any h∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. Corollary 2 shows that the set 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk can be partitioned into disjoint union of ”orbits” relatively to this action and each orbit contains at least one initial element (such that every element of the orbit is its image but this element has no preimages of smaller degree). Besides, this initial element is determined up to affine transformations and can be chosen irreducible.

3. A factorization theorem

Let us assume in this section that our ground field 𝕜\Bbbk is algebraically closed. Theorem 1 states that for a closed polynomial h∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] the polynomial h+λh+\lambda may be reducible only for finitely many λ∈𝕜\lambda\in\Bbbk. Denote by E⁡(h)E(h) the set of λ∈𝕜\lambda\in\Bbbk such that h+λh+\lambda is reducible and by e⁡(h)e(h) the cardinality of this set. Stein’s inequality claims that

e⁡(h)<deg⁡f.e(h)<\deg f.

Now for any λ∈𝕜\lambda\in\Bbbk consider a decomposition

h+λ=∏i=1n⁡(λ,h)hλ,idλ,ih+\lambda=\prod_{i=1}^{n(\lambda,h)}h_{\lambda,i}^{d_{\lambda,i}}

with hλ,ih_{\lambda,i} being irreducible. A more precise version of Stein’s inequality is given in the next theorem.

Theorem 2 (Stein-Lorenzini-Najib’s Inequality).

Let h∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]h\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] be a closed polynomial. Then

∑λ(n⁡(λ,h)−1)<minλ⁡(∑ideg⁡(hλ,i)).\sum_{\lambda}(n(\lambda,h)-1)<\min_{\lambda}(\sum_{i}\deg(h_{\lambda,i})).

This inequality has rather long history. Stein [19] proved his inequality in characteristic zero for n=2n=2. For any nn over 𝕜=ℂ\Bbbk=\mathbb{C} this inequality was proved in [4]. In 1993, Lorenzini [10] obtained the inequality as in Theorem 2 in any characteristic, but only for n=2n=2 (see also [8] and [20]). Finally, in [11] the proof for an arbitrary nn was reduced to the case n=2n=2.

Now take any f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk, μ∈𝕜\mu\in\Bbbk and consider a decomposition

f+μ=α⋅∏i=1n⁡(μ,f)fμ,idμ,if+\mu=\alpha\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{n(\mu,f)}f_{\mu,i}^{d_{\mu,i}}

with α∈𝕜×\alpha\in\Bbbk^{\times} and fμ,if_{\mu,i} being irreducible.

Let us state the main result of this section.

Theorem 3.

Let f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk. There exists a finite subset E(f)={μ1,…,μe⁡(f)∣μi∈𝕜}E(f)=\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{e(f)}\mid\mu_{i}\in\Bbbk\} with e⁡(f)<deg⁡fe(f)<\deg f such that

  1. (1)

    for any μ∉E⁡(f)\mu\notin E(f) one has f+μ=α⋅fμ,1⋅fμ,2⋯fμ,kf+\mu=\alpha\cdot f_{\mu,1}\cdot f_{\mu,2}\cdot\cdot\cdot f_{\mu,k}, where all fμ,if_{\mu,i} are irreducible and fμ,i−fμ,j∈𝕜f_{\mu,i}-f_{\mu,j}\in\Bbbk;

  2. (2)

    fμ,i−fν,j∈𝕜×f_{\mu,i}-f_{\nu,j}\in\Bbbk^{\times} for any μ,ν∉E⁡(f)\mu,\nu\notin E(f) with ν≠μ\nu\neq\mu; in particular, the degree d=deg⁡(fμ,i)d=\deg(f_{\mu,i}) does not depend on ii and μ\mu;

  3. (3)

    deg⁡(fμ,i)≤d\deg(f_{\mu,i})\leq d for any μ∈𝕜\mu\in\Bbbk;

  4. (4)
    ∑μ(n⁡(μ,f)−deg⁡(f)d)<minμ⁡(∑i=1n⁡(μ,f)deg⁡(fμ,i)).\sum_{\mu}(n(\mu,f)-\frac{\deg(f)}{d})<\min_{\mu}(\sum_{i=1}^{n(\mu,f)}\deg(f_{\mu,i})).
Proof.

Let hh be the generative polynomial of ff and f=F⁡(h)f=F(h). Then

F(h)+μ=α⋅(h+λμ,1)⋯(h+λμ,k)F(h)+\mu=\alpha\cdot(h+\lambda_{\mu,1})\cdot\cdot\cdot(h+\lambda_{\mu,k})

for some λμ,1,…,λμ,k∈𝕜\lambda_{\mu,1},\dots,\lambda_{\mu,k}\in\Bbbk. Hence for any μ\mu with λμ,1,…,λμ,k∉E⁡(h)\lambda_{\mu,1},\dots,\lambda_{\mu,k}\notin E(h) we have a decomposition of f+μf+\mu as in (1). Note that λμ,i≠λν,j\lambda_{\mu,i}\neq\lambda_{\nu,j} for μ≠ν\mu\neq\nu. This proves (2) with d=deg⁡(h)d=\deg(h) and gives the inequalities

e⁡(f)≤e⁡(h)<deg⁡(h)≤deg⁡(f).e(f)\leq e(h)<\deg(h)\leq\deg(f).

Any fμ,if_{\mu,i} is a divisor of some h+λh+\lambda. This implies (3).

Finally, (4) may be obtained as:

∑μ(n⁡(μ,f)−deg⁡(f)d)≤∑λ(n⁡(λ,h)−1)<\sum_{\mu}(n(\mu,f)-\frac{\deg(f)}{d})\leq\sum_{\lambda}(n(\lambda,h)-1)<
<minλ⁡(∑ideg⁡(hλ,i))≤minμ⁡(∑jdeg⁡(fμ,j)).<\min_{\lambda}(\sum_{i}\deg(h_{\lambda,i}))\leq\min_{\mu}(\sum_{j}\deg(f_{\mu,j})).

∎

It follows from the proof of Theorem 3 that

    if ff is not closed, then e⁡(f)<12​deg⁡(f)e(f)<\frac{1}{2}\deg(f).

Example 2.

Take f⁡(x1,x2)=x12​x24−2​x12​x23+x12​x22+2​x1​x23−2​x1​x22+x22+1f(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{4}-2x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{3}+x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{2}+2x_{1}x_{2}^{3}-2x_{1}x_{2}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+1.

Here h=x1​x2​(x2−1)+x2h=x_{1}x_{2}(x_{2}-1)+x_{2} and F⁡(t)=t2+1F(t)=t^{2}+1. It is easy to check that E⁡(h)={0,−1}E(h)=\{0,-1\}, thus E⁡(f)={−1,−2}E(f)=\{-1,-2\}. We have decompositions:

μ=−1:f−1=x22​(x1​x2−x1+1)2;\mu=-1:\ \ f-1=x_{2}^{2}(x_{1}x_{2}-x_{1}+1)^{2};

λ2=−1−μ.\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \lambda^{2}=-1-\mu.

In this case deg⁡(f)=6\deg(f)=6, d=3d=3, ∑μ(n⁡(μ,f)−2)=1\sum_{\mu}(n(\mu,f)-2)=1 and

minμ⁡(∑ideg⁡(fμ,i))=min⁡{3,6,6}=3.\min_{\mu}(\sum_{i}\deg(f_{\mu,i}))=\min\{3,6,6\}=3.

4. Saturated subalgebras and invariants of finite groups

Let 𝕜\Bbbk be a field.

Definition 4.

A subalgebra A⊆𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]A\subseteq\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is said to be saturated if for any f∈A∖𝕜f\in A\setminus\Bbbk the generative polynomial of ff is contained in AA.

Clearly, the intersection of a family of saturated subalgebras in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is again a saturated subalgebra. So we may define the saturation S⁡(A)S(A) of a subalgebra AA as the minimal saturated subalgebra containing AA.

If AA is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], then AA is saturated. By Theorem 1, if A=𝕜⁡[f]A=\Bbbk[f], then the converse is true. Moreover, the converse is true if AA is a monomial subalgebra. In order to prove it, consider a submonoid P⁡(A)P(A) in ℤ≥0n\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n} consisting of multidegrees of all monomials in AA. Then monomials corresponding to elements of the ”saturated” semigroup P′​(A)=(ℚ≥0​P​(A))∩ℤ≥0nP^{\prime}(A)=(\mathbb{Q}_{\geq 0}P(A))\cap\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n} are generative elements of AA. On the other hand, it is a basic fact of toric geometry that the monomial subalgebra corresponding to P′​(A)P^{\prime}(A) is integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], see for example [6, Sec. 2.1].

Now we come from monomial to homogeneous saturated subalgebras. The degree of monomials deg⁡(α​x1i1​…​xnin)=i1+…​in\deg(\alpha x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{i_{n}})=i_{1}+\dots i_{n} defines a ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}-grading on the polynomial algebra 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. Recall that a subalgebra A⊂𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]A\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is called homogeneous if for any element a∈Aa\in A all its homogeneous components belong to AA.

Consider a subgroup G⊂GLn​(𝕜)G\subset\rm{GL}_{n}(\Bbbk). The linear action G:𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]G:\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] determines the homogeneous subalgebra 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} of GG-invariant polynomials.

Theorem 4.

Let G⊆GLn​(𝕜)G\subseteq\rm{GL}_{n}(\Bbbk) be a finite subgroup. Then the subalgebra A=𝕜​[x1,…,xn]GA=\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} is saturated in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] if and only if GG admits no non-trivial homomorphisms G→𝕜×G\to\Bbbk^{\times}.

Proof.

Assume that there is a non-trivial homomorphism ϕ:G→𝕜×\phi:G\to\Bbbk^{\times}. Let GϕG_{\phi} be the kernel of ϕ\phi and Gϕ=G/GϕG^{\phi}=G/G_{\phi}. Then GϕG^{\phi} is a finite cyclic group of some order kk and it may be identified with a subgroup of 𝕜×\Bbbk^{\times}.

Lemma 6.

Let HH be a cyclic subgroup of order kk in 𝕜×\Bbbk^{\times}. Then any finite dimensional (over 𝕜\Bbbk) HH-module WW is a direct sum of one-dimensional submodules.

Proof.

The polynomial Xk−1X^{k}-1 annihilates the linear operator PP in GL⁡(W)\rm{GL}(W) corresponding to a generator of HH. By assumption, Xk−1X^{k}-1 is a product of kk non-proportional linear factors in 𝕜⁡[X]\Bbbk[X]. This shows that the operator PP is diagonalizable. ∎

Lemma 7.

Let H⊂GH\subset G be a proper subgroup. Then 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]H≠𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{H}\neq\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}.

Proof.

Let KK be a field and GG a finite group of its automorphisms. By Artin’s Theorem [9, Ch.VI, Th.1.8], KG⊂KK^{G}\subset K is a Galois extension and
[K:KG]=|G|[K:K^{G}]=|G|. This implies 𝕜​(x1,…,xn)H≠𝕜​(x1,…,xn)G\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})^{H}\neq\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})^{G}. The implication

fh∈𝕜​(x1,…,xn)G⟹f​∏g∈G,g≠eg⋅fh​∏g∈G,g≠eg⋅f∈𝕜​(x1,…,xn)G\frac{f}{h}\in\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})^{G}\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{f\prod_{g\in G,g\neq e}g\cdot f}{h\prod_{g\in G,g\neq e}g\cdot f}\in\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})^{G}

shows that 𝕜​(x1,…,xn)G\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})^{G} (resp. 𝕜​(x1,…,xn)H\Bbbk(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})^{H}) is the quotient field of 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} (resp. 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]H\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{H}), thus 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]H≠𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{H}\neq\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}. ∎

Now we may take a finite-dimensional GG-submodule W⊂𝕜​[x1,…,xn]GϕW\subset\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G_{\phi}} which is not contained in 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}. Then WW is a GϕG^{\phi}-module. By Lemma 6, one may find a GϕG^{\phi}-eigenvector h∈Wh\in W, h∉𝕜​[x1,…,xn]Gh\notin\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}. Then hk∈𝕜​[x1,…,xn]Gh^{k}\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} and 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} is not saturated.

Conversely, assume that any homomorphism χ:G→𝕜\chi:G\to\Bbbk is trivial. If hh is a generative element of a polynomial f∈𝕜​[x1,…,xn]Gf\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}, then for any g∈Gg\in G the element g⋅hg\cdot h is also a generative element of ff. By Corollary 1, the generative element is unique up to affine transformation. Without loss of generality we can assume that the constant term of hh is zero. Then the element g⋅hg\cdot h has obviously zero constant term and by Corollary 1 this element is proportional to hh for any g∈Gg\in G. Thus GG acts on the line ⟨h⟩\langle h\rangle via some character. But any character of GG is trivial, so h∈𝕜​[x1,…,xn]Gh\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}, and 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} is saturated. ∎

Remark 5.

Since all coefficients of the polynomial

Ff​(T)=∏g∈G(T−g⋅f)F_{f}(T)=\prod_{g\in G}(T-g\cdot f)

are in 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}, any element f∈𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] is integral over 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G}. Thus Theorem 4 provides many saturated homogeneous subalgebras that are not integrally closed in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}].

Corollary 3.

Assume that 𝕜\Bbbk is algebraically closed and char𝕜=0\mathop{\mathrm{char}}\Bbbk=0.

  1. (1)

    The subalgebra 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} is saturated in 𝕜⁡[x1,…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] if and only if GG coincides with its commutant.

  2. (2)

    The saturation of 𝕜​[x1,…,xn]G\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]^{G} is 𝕜⁡[x1​…,xn]\Bbbk[x_{1}\dots,x_{n}] if and only if GG is solvable.

Example 3.

In general, the saturation S⁡(A)S(A) is not generated by generative elements of elements of AA. Indeed, take any field 𝕜\Bbbk that contains a primitive root of unit of degree six. Let G=S3G=S_{3} be the permutation group acting naturally on 𝕜⁡[x1,x2,x3]\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}] and A3⊂S3A_{3}\subset S_{3} be the alternating subgroup. The proof of Theorem 4 shows that any generative element of an S3S_{3}-invariant is an S3S_{3}-semiinvariant and thus belongs to 𝕜​[x1,x2,x3]A3\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]^{A_{3}}. On the other hand, S⁡(𝕜​[x1,x2,x3]S3)=𝕜⁡[x1,x2,x3]S(\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}]^{S_{3}})=\Bbbk[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}].

Example 4.

It follows from Theorem 4 that the property of a subalgebra to be saturated is not preserved under field extensions. Let us give an explicit example of this effect.

Let 𝕜=ℝ\Bbbk=\mathbb{R} and GG be the cyclic group of order three acting on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} by rotations. We begin with calculation of generators of the algebra of invariants ℝ​[x,y]G\mathbb{R}[x,y]^{G}. Consider the complex polynomial algebra ℂ⁡[x,y]=ℝ⁡[x,y]⊕i​ℝ​[x,y]\mathbb{C}[x,y]=\mathbb{R}[x,y]\oplus\text{i}\mathbb{R}[x,y] with the natural GG-action. Then ℂ​[x,y]G=ℝ​[x,y]G⊕i​ℝ​[x,y]G\mathbb{C}[x,y]^{G}=\mathbb{R}[x,y]^{G}\oplus\text{i}\mathbb{R}[x,y]^{G}. Put z=x+i​yz=x+\text{i}y, z¯=x−i​y\overline{z}=x-\text{i}y. Clearly, ℂ⁡[x,y]=ℂ⁡[z,z¯]\mathbb{C}[x,y]=\mathbb{C}[z,\overline{z}], and GG acts on z,z¯z,\overline{z} as z→ϵ​zz\to\epsilon z, z¯→ϵ¯​z¯\overline{z}\to\overline{\epsilon}\overline{z}, where ϵ3=1\epsilon^{3}=1. This implies ℂ​[z,z¯]G=ℂ⁡[f1,f2,f3]\mathbb{C}[z,\overline{z}]^{G}=\mathbb{C}[f_{1},f_{2},f_{3}] with f1=z3f_{1}=z^{3}, f2=z¯3f_{2}=\overline{z}^{3} and f3=z​z¯f_{3}=z\overline{z}. Finally, ℝ​[x,y]G=ℝ⁡[Re​(fi),Im​(fi);i=1,2,3]=ℝ⁡[x3−3​x​y2,y3−3​x2​y,x2+y2]\mathbb{R}[x,y]^{G}=\mathbb{R}[\text{Re}(f_{i}),\text{Im}(f_{i});\ i=1,2,3]=\mathbb{R}[x^{3}-3xy^{2},y^{3}-3x^{2}y,x^{2}+y^{2}].

By Theorem 4, the subalgebra ℝ​[x,y]G\mathbb{R}[x,y]^{G} is saturated in ℝ⁡[x,y]\mathbb{R}[x,y]. On the other hand, the subalgebra ℂ⁡[x3−3​x​y2,y3−3​x2​y,x2+y2]\mathbb{C}[x^{3}-3xy^{2},y^{3}-3x^{2}y,x^{2}+y^{2}] contains x3−3​x​y2+i​(y3−3​x2​y)=(x−i​y)3x^{3}-3xy^{2}+\text{i}(y^{3}-3x^{2}y)=(x-\text{i}y)^{3}.

5. An algorithmic approach to closed polynomials

Let us assume in this section that char​𝕜=0{\rm char\ }\Bbbk=0. Fix a homogeneous monomial order ≻\succ on the set M⁡(n)M(n) of monomials in x1,…,xnx_{1},\dots,x_{n}, i.e., a total order satisfying the following conditions:

  1. (i)

    m≻1m\succ 1 for any m∈M⁡(n)∖{1}m\in M(n)\setminus\{1\};

  2. (ii)

    m1≻m2m_{1}\succ m_{2} implies m​m1≻m​m2mm_{1}\succ mm_{2} for all m,m1,m2∈M⁡(n)m,m_{1},m_{2}\in M(n);

  3. (iii)

    if deg⁡m1>deg⁡m2\deg m_{1}>\deg m_{2}, then m1≻m2m_{1}\succ m_{2}.

Take a polynomial f∈𝕜[x1,…,xn]∖𝕜]f\in\Bbbk[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\setminus\Bbbk] such that the leading coefficient of ff (with respect to ≻\succ) is 1 and f⁡(0,…,0)=0f(0,\dots,0)=0. Let hh be the generative polynomial of ff satisfying the same assumptions. One has f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) with FF having the highest coefficient equals 1 and F⁡(0)=0F(0)=0.

Define the multiplicity of a monomial m=x1i1​…​xninm=x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{i_{n}} as d⁡(m)=G​C​D​(i1,…,in)d(m)=GCD(i_{1},\dots,i_{n}). If f=F⁡(g)f=F(g), deg⁡(F)=k\deg(F)=k, and f¯\overline{f} is the leading monomial of ff, then d⁡(f¯)d(\overline{f}) is divisible by kk. In particular, if d⁡(f¯)=1d(\overline{f})=1, then ff is closed.

Below we give an algorithm computing the generative polynomial of a given polynomial f⁡(x1,…,xn)f(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}).

Step 1. Find a sequence D⁡(f)=(d1>⋯>ds)D(f)=(d_{1}>\dots>d_{s}) of all divisors of d⁡(f¯)d(\overline{f}) greater than 1. Put j=1j=1.

Step 2. Take the divisor k=djk=d_{j}. Put m1=x1i1′​…​xnin′m_{1}=x_{1}^{i_{1}^{\prime}}\dots x_{n}^{i_{n}^{\prime}}, where ip′=ipki_{p}^{\prime}=\frac{i_{p}}{k}. Let m1≻m2≻⋯≻mN≻1m_{1}\succ m_{2}\succ\dots\succ m_{N}\succ 1 be the set of all monomials that do not exceed m1m_{1}. Consider h=m1+α2​m2+⋯+αN​mNh=m_{1}+\alpha_{2}m_{2}+\dots+\alpha_{N}m_{N} with indeterminate coefficients αj\alpha_{j}. Let us find αj\alpha_{j} inductively. Suppose that the coefficient in ff of the monomial m1k−1​mjm_{1}^{k-1}m_{j} equals bjb_{j}. Then α2=b2k\alpha_{2}=\frac{b_{2}}{k} and, for j=3,…,Nj=3,\dots,N, αj=bj−Kjk\alpha_{j}=\frac{b_{j}-K_{j}}{k}, where KjK_{j} is the coefficient of m1k−1​mjm_{1}^{k-1}m_{j} in (m1+α2​m2+⋯+αj−1​mj−1)k(m_{1}+\alpha_{2}m_{2}+\dots+\alpha_{j-1}m_{j-1})^{k}.

Step 3. Put F⁡(t)=tk+β1​tk−1+⋯+βk−1​tF(t)=t^{k}+\beta_{1}t^{k-1}+\dots+\beta_{k-1}t with indeterminate coefficients βl\beta_{l}. Assuming that f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) with hh found at Step 2, one may calculate βl\beta_{l} inductively (from l=1l=1 to k−1k-1) looking at the coefficient of m1k−lm_{1}^{k-l}.

Step 4. Check the equality f=F⁡(h)f=F(h) with hh and FF found at Steps 2 and 3 respectively. If the equality holds, then hh is the generative polynomial for ff. (Indeed, if h=F1​(h1)h=F_{1}(h_{1}) with deg⁡F1>1\deg F_{1}>1, then f=F⁡(F1​(h1))f=F(F_{1}(h_{1})) and this expression corresponds to the divisor deg⁡F⁡(F1​(t))>k\deg F(F_{1}(t))>k of d⁡(f¯)d(\overline{f}), a contradiction.) If the equality does not hold and j<sj<s, then put j:=j+1j:=j+1 and go to Step 2. If the equality does not hold and j=sj=s, then h=fh=f is the generative polynomial of ff.

Example 5.

Consider the case n=2n=2 and take the homogeneous lexicographic order with x1≻x2x_{1}\succ x_{2}. For f⁡(x1,x2)=x14+2​x12​x2+x22f(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}^{4}+2x_{1}^{2}x_{2}+x_{2}^{2} one has f¯=x14\overline{f}=x_{1}^{4}, d⁡(m)=4d(m)=4 and D⁡(f)=(4,2)D(f)=(4,2).

1) k=d1=4k=d_{1}=4. Here m1=x1m_{1}=x_{1}, m2=x2m_{2}=x_{2} and N=2N=2. One easily find that α2=0\alpha_{2}=0, hence h=x1h=x_{1}. Moreover, F⁡(t)=t4+β1​t3+β2​t2+β3​tF(t)=t^{4}+\beta_{1}t^{3}+\beta_{2}t^{2}+\beta_{3}t. Fulfilling Step 3, we get β1=β2=β3=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=0. So, the equality f=F⁡(h)=x14f=F(h)=x_{1}^{4} does not hold.

2) k=d2=2k=d_{2}=2. Here m1=x12m_{1}=x_{1}^{2} and

h=x12+α2​x1​x2+α3​x22+α4​x1+α5​x2.h=x_{1}^{2}+\alpha_{2}x_{1}x_{2}+\alpha_{3}x_{2}^{2}+\alpha_{4}x_{1}+\alpha_{5}x_{2}.

Using Step 2, we get α2=α3=α4=0\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}=\alpha_{4}=0 and α2=1\alpha_{2}=1. Put F⁡(t)=t2+β1​tF(t)=t^{2}+\beta_{1}t, we find β1=0\beta_{1}=0 and the equality f=F⁡(h)=(x12+x2)2f=F(h)=(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2})^{2} holds. So the generative polynomial for ff is h=x12+x2h=x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}.

Remark 6.

If char𝕜=p\mathop{\mathrm{char}}\Bbbk=p and G​C​D​(p,d⁡(f¯))=1GCD(p,d(\overline{f}))=1, then our algorithm also works.

Finally, let us present some observations that may speed up the above algorithm. With any term α​x1i1​…​xnin\alpha x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{i_{n}}, α≠0\alpha\neq 0, of the polynomial ff one may associate an integral point (i1,…,in)(i_{1},\dots,i_{n}) in the real vector space ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Let N⁡(f)N(f) be the Newton polytope of ff, i.e., the convex hull of all (i1,…,in)(i_{1},\dots,i_{n}). Consider the set VV of all vertices of N⁡(f)N(f). Let

V0={(i1,…,in)∈V∣∀(j1,…,jn)≠(i1,…,in)∈V∃s:is>js}.V_{0}=\{(i_{1},\dots,i_{n})\in V\mid\forall\ (j_{1},\dots,j_{n})\neq(i_{1},\dots,i_{n})\in V\ \exists\ s\ :\ i_{s}>j_{s}\}.
Lemma 8.

The elements of V0V_{0} parametrize terms of ff that are the leading terms with respect to some monomial order on M⁡(n)M(n).

Proof.

If js≥isj_{s}\geq i_{s} for any ss, then x1j1​…​xnjn≻x1i1​…​xninx_{1}^{j_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{j_{n}}\succ x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{i_{n}} for any monomial order ≻\succ. Conversely, if (i1,…,in)∈V0(i_{1},\dots,i_{n})\in V_{0}, then N⁡(f)−(i1,…,in)N(f)-(i_{1},\dots,i_{n}) intersects the positive octant of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} only at zero. Hence there is a linear function l⁡(z)=ω1​z1+⋯+ωn​znl(z)=\omega_{1}z_{1}+\dots+\omega_{n}z_{n} such that the hyperplane l⁡(z)=0l(z)=0 separates the positive octant and N⁡(f)−(i1,…,in)N(f)-(i_{1},\dots,i_{n}), and all ωi\omega_{i} are positive. (Here ziz_{i} are coordinates in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.) Moreover, one may assume that ωi\omega_{i} are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q}.

With any sequence Ω=(ω1,…,ωn)\Omega=(\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{n}) of positive real numbers that are linearly independent over ℚ\mathbb{Q} one may associate a monomial (non-homogeneous) order ≻Ω\succ_{\Omega} defined as

x1i1…xnin≻Ωx1j1…xnjn⇔ω1i1+⋯+ωnin>ω1j1+⋯+ωnjn.x_{1}^{i_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{i_{n}}\succ_{\Omega}x_{1}^{j_{1}}\dots x_{n}^{j_{n}}\Leftrightarrow\omega_{1}i_{1}+\dots+\omega_{n}i_{n}>\omega_{1}j_{1}+\dots+\omega_{n}j_{n}.

Clearly, (i1,…,in)(i_{1},\dots,i_{n}) represents the leading term with respect to ≻Ω\succ_{\Omega} defined by the coefficients of l⁡(z)l(z). ∎

Now for any v∈V0v\in V_{0}, let mvm_{v} be the leading monomial of ff with respect to the corresponding order, and d1​(f)=G​C​D​(d⁡(mv)∣v∈V0)d_{1}(f)=GCD(d(m_{v})\mid v\in V_{0}). Considering the leading terms of F⁡(h)F(h) with respect to all possible monomial orders, one shows that the sequence D⁡(f)D(f) at Step 1 may be replaced by the sequence D1​(f)=(d~1>⋯>d~p)D_{1}(f)=(\tilde{d}_{1}>\dots>\tilde{d}_{p}) of all divisors of d1​(f)d_{1}(f) greater than 1.

Let us return to Example 5. Here V=V0={(4,0),(0,2)}V=V_{0}=\{(4,0),(0,2)\} and D1​(f)=(2)D_{1}(f)=(2). Hence the case k=4k=4 may be excluded.
